children.translated_text: Om. Homage to <s>Śukra</s> and <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.

children.text: pṛthivyā lābhe pālane ca yāvantyarthaśāstrāṇi pūrvācāryaiḥ prasthāpitāni prāyaśastāni saṃhṛtyaikam idam arthaśāstraṃ kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Having generally gathered together all the treatises on artha that earlier teachers had established for acquiring and protecting the earth, this single <s>Arthaśāstra</s> has been composed.
This is the summary of its sections and books.
Summary of the sciences.
Summary concerning the elders.
Conquest of the senses.
The selection of ministers.
The selection of counselors and the royal priest.
Knowing the purity or impurity of ministers through tests.
Deployment of secret agents.
Protecting the factions to be acted upon and not to be acted upon in one's own territory.
Winning over the factions to be acted upon and not to be acted upon in another's territory.
The office of counsel.
Deployment of envoys.
Protection of royal princes.
Conduct toward one who is confined.
Livelihood for one who is confined.
Royal supervision.
Supervision of the inner apartments.
Personal security.
Thus ends the first book, concerning discipline.
Settlement of the countryside.
Filling gaps in the land.
Construction of forts.
Layout of a fort.
The store-superintendent's work of accumulation.
The collector-general's establishment of revenue in the record office.
The office of accounting.
Recovery of revenue embezzled by officials.
Examination of what has been expended.
The office of royal orders.
Examination of jewels fit to enter the treasury.
Starting mines and workshops.
The superintendent of gold in the mint.
The activity of goldsmiths in the market street.
The superintendent of storehouses.
The superintendent of merchandise.
The superintendent of forest products.
The superintendent of weapons.
The accuracy of weights and measures.
Measurement of place and time.
The superintendent of customs duties.
The superintendent of thread and textiles.
The superintendent of crown agriculture.
The superintendent of liquor.
The superintendent of slaughterhouses.
The superintendent of courtesans.
The superintendent of ships.
The superintendent of cattle.
The superintendent of horses.
The superintendent of elephants.
The superintendent of chariots.
The superintendent of infantry.
The activity of the commander-in-chief.
The superintendent of seals and passports.
The superintendent of pastures.
The activity of the collector-general.
Agents disguised as householders, merchants, and ascetics.
Deployment by the city superintendent.
Thus ends the second book, the activity of superintendents.
Establishment of legal procedure.
Recording the grounds of litigation.
Matters connected with marriage.
Division of inheritance.
Matters concerning house-sites and property.
Non-performance of an agreement.
Recovery of debts.
Matters concerning deposits.
Rules for slaves and hired laborers.
Undertaking business in partnership.
Repentance over what has been sold or bought.
Failure to restore what has been given.
Sale by one who is not the owner.
The relation between property and its owner.
Violent assault.
Verbal abuse.
Physical assault.
Gambling and wagering.
Miscellaneous matters.
Thus ends the third book, concerning the courts of law.
Protection of artisans.
Protection of merchants.
Remedying sudden calamities.
Guarding against those who live by secret means.
Exposing young men through agents disguised as accomplished adepts.
Arrest on the basis of suspicion, appearance, and deed.
Examination of sudden death.
Questioning about speech and action.
Protection of all offices.
Commutation for the cutting off of a limb.
Rules for ordinary and extraordinary punishments.
Offenses against maidens.
Punishments for transgressions.
Thus ends the fourth book, the removal of thorns.
Matters concerning officers of punishment.
Gathering wealth into the treasury.
Maintenance of servants.
Conduct of dependents.
Conduct according to agreements and custom.
Restoration of the kingdom.
Single sovereignty.
Thus ends the fifth book, conduct in service.
The excellences of the state constituents.
Peace and exertion.
Thus ends the sixth book, the source of the circle of kings.
Summary of the six measures of policy.
Determination of decline, stability, and growth.
Conduct when seeking shelter or alliance.
Application of the policies toward equal, inferior, and superior kings.
Treaties for the weaker party.
Remaining quiet after making war.
Remaining quiet after making peace.
Marching after making war.
Marching after making peace.
Marching together.
Consideration of attacking the target of an expedition and the enemy.
Causes of decline, greed, and disaffection.
Consideration of the state constituents collectively and individually.
Matters concerning a combined march.
Treaties with stipulated terms, without stipulated terms, and with withdrawal.
Treaties and advances involving a dual policy.
Conduct toward the target of an expedition.
Special kinds of allies to be supported.
Treaties concerning allies, gold, land, and works.
Consideration of the rear-attacker.
Making up a deficiency in power.
Causes of obstruction after making war with a stronger power.
Conduct of one brought under force.
Conduct of one who brings force to bear.
The act of making a treaty.
Release from an agreement.
Conduct of the middle king.
Conduct of the neutral king.
Conduct in the circle of kings.
Thus ends the seventh book, the six measures of policy.
The class of calamities affecting the state constituents.
Consideration of calamities affecting the king and kingdom.
The class of personal calamities.
The class of oppressions.
The class of obstructions.
The class of blockages in the treasury.
The class of calamities affecting allies.
Thus ends the eighth book, concerning calamities.
Knowledge of strength and weakness with respect to power, place, time, and forces.
Times for an expedition.
Times for assembling forces.
Qualities of military preparation.
Action against an opposing force.
Consideration of revolt in the rear.
Remedies for revolts among external and internal state constituents.
Consideration of loss, expense, and gain.
External and internal dangers.
Dangers connected with corrupt elements and enemies.
Dangers connected with gain, harm, and uncertainty.
Successes arising from alternative means against them.
Thus ends the ninth book, the work of one intending to march.
Establishment of the military camp.
The march of the military camp.
Protection against calamities of the army and the times for assaults.
Alternatives in deceptive warfare.
Encouraging one's own army.
Engagement of one's own force with the enemy's force.
Battlefields.
Operations of infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants.
Division of formations with wings, flanks, and front before the army.
Division of strong and weak troops.
Battles of infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants.
Deploying line, curved, circular, and dispersed battle formations.
Establishing the counter-formation against it.
Thus [ends] the tenth book, 'Concerning War.'
The means of creating dissension.
Secret punishments.
Thus [ends] the eleventh book, 'The Conduct of Confederacies.'
The work of an envoy.
War by counsel.
The killing of the army chiefs.
The stirring up of the circle of kings.
The employment of weapons, fire, and poison.
The destruction of supply trains, reserves, and reinforcements.
Deception by stratagem.
Deception by force.
A single victory.
Thus [ends] the twelfth book, 'Concerning the Weaker King.'
Secret instigation.
Weakening by stratagem.
The posting of secret agents.
The operations of siege.
The assault.
Pacification after acquisition.
Thus [ends] the thirteenth book, 'Means for Taking a Fort.'
The application of means for striking the enemy's forces.
Deception.
Countermeasures against injury to one's own forces.
Thus [ends] the fourteenth book, 'The Secret Means.'
The methodological devices of the treatise.
Thus [ends] the fifteenth book, 'Methodological Devices of the Treatise.'
The enumeration of the treatise: fifteen books, one hundred and eighty topics, one hundred and fifty chapters, and six thousand verses.
Easy to grasp and understand, with the meaning of principles and terms made definite,
this treatise was composed by <s>Kauṭilya</s>, freed from prolix extension.
<s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (critical inquiry), <s>trayī</s> (the three Vedas), <s>vārttā</s> (agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade), and <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (the policy of punishment) are the sciences.
The <s>Mānava</s> teachers say: the three Vedas, vārttā, and daṇḍanīti are the sciences.
For ānvīkṣikī is only a special branch of the three Vedas.
The followers of <s>Bṛhaspati</s> say: vārttā and daṇḍanīti are the sciences.
For the three Vedas are merely a screen for one who knows the course of worldly life.
The followers of <s>Uśanas</s> say: daṇḍanīti alone is the science.
For in it all undertakings of the sciences are bound up.
<s>Kauṭilya</s> says: there are exactly four sciences.

children.text: tābhir dharmārthau yad vidyāt tad vidyānāṃ vidyātvam ||
children.translated_text: Since through them one knows <s>dharma</s> (normative duty) and <s>artha</s> (material advantage), that is what makes them sciences.
<s>Sāṃkhya</s>, <s>Yoga</s>, and <s>Lokāyata</s> constitute ānvīkṣikī.

children.text: dharmādharmau trayyām arthānarthau vārttāyāṃ nayānayau daṇḍanītyāṃ balābale ca etāsāṃ hetubhir anvīkṣamāṇā lokasya upakaroti vyasane 'bhyudaye ca buddhim avasthāpayati prajñāvākyakriyāvaiśāradyaṃ ca karoti ||
children.translated_text: By examining with reasons dharma and adharma in the three Vedas, artha and anartha in vārttā, right policy and wrong policy in daṇḍanīti, and the strengths and weaknesses of these, ānvīkṣikī benefits the world in calamity and prosperity, steadies the intellect, and produces skill in understanding, speech, and action.
It is the lamp of all sciences and the means for all actions;
ānvīkṣikī is always regarded as the support of all dharmas.
The <s>Sāma</s>, <s>Ṛg</s>, and <s>Yajur</s> Vedas are the threefold Veda.
And the <s>Atharvaveda</s> and the <s>Itihāsaveda</s> are also Vedas.

children.text: śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chandovicitir jyotiṣam iti cāṅgāni ||
children.translated_text: Phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, etymology, metrical analysis, and jyotiṣa are the auxiliary limbs.

children.text: eṣa trayīdharmaścaturṇāṃ varṇānām āśramāṇāṃ ca svadharmasthāpanād aupakārikaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This dharma of the threefold Veda is helpful because it establishes the proper duties of the four varṇas and the āśramas.

children.text: svadharmo brāhmaṇasya adhyayanam adhyāpanaṃ yajanaṃ yājanaṃ dānaṃ pratigrahaśca ||
children.translated_text: The svadharma of a brāhmaṇa is study, teaching, sacrificing for himself, sacrificing for others, giving, and receiving gifts.

children.text: kṣatriyasyādhyayanaṃ yajanaṃ dānaṃ śastrājīvo bhūtarakṣaṇaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: For a kṣatriya it is study, sacrificing, giving, livelihood by arms, and protection of beings.

children.text: vaiśyasyādhyayanaṃ yajanaṃ dānaṃ kṛṣipāśupālye vaṇijyā ca ||
children.translated_text: For a vaiśya it is study, sacrificing, giving, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.
For a śūdra it is service to the twice-born, vārttā, and the work of artisans and performers.

children.text: gṛhasthasya svadharmājīvastulyair asamānarṣibhir vaivāhyam ṛtugāmitvaṃ devapitratithipūjā bhṛtyeṣu tyāgaḥ śeṣabhojanaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: For a householder it is livelihood according to his own dharma, marriage with equals whose ancestral seers are not the same, intercourse in the proper season, worship of gods, ancestors, and guests, generosity toward servants, and eating what remains.

children.text: brahmacāriṇaḥ svādhyāyo 'gnikāryābhiṣekau bhaikṣavratitvam ācārye prāṇāntikī vṛttistadabhāve guruputre sabrahmacāriṇi vā ||
children.translated_text: For a brahmacārin it is recitation of scripture, duties to the sacred fire and ritual bathing, living by alms, and conduct toward the teacher until death; in the teacher's absence, toward the teacher's son or a fellow student.

children.text: vānaprasthasya brahmacaryaṃ bhūmau śayyā jaṭājinadhāraṇam agnihotrābhiṣekau devatāpitratithipūjā vanyaścāhāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a forest-dweller it is celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair and deerskin, agnihotra and ritual bathing, worship of deities, ancestors, and guests, and food from the wild.

children.text: parivrājakasya jitendriyatvam anārambho niṣkiṃcanatvaṃ saṅgatyāgo bhaikṣavratam anekatrāraṇye ca vāso bāhyābhyantaraṃ ca śaucam ||
children.translated_text: For a wandering ascetic it is mastery of the senses, undertaking no enterprise, possessionlessness, abandonment of attachment, living by alms, dwelling in many places and in the forest, and purity both external and internal.

children.text: sarveṣām ahiṃsā satyaṃ śaucam anasūyānṛśaṃsyaṃ kṣamā ca ||
children.translated_text: For all, there are non-injury, truthfulness, purity, freedom from envy, non-cruelty, and patience.
One's own dharma leads to heaven and to endlessness.
If it is transgressed, the world would be destroyed through mixture.

children.text: tasmāt svadharmaṃ bhūtānāṃ rājā na vyabhicārayet
children.translated_text: Therefore the king should not cause beings to deviate from their own dharma;

children.text: svadharmaṃ saṃdadhāno hi pretya ceha ca nandati ||
children.translated_text: for, keeping them joined to their own dharma, he rejoices both after death and here.
When the boundaries of the Āryas are duly established and the order of varṇa and āśrama has been made firm,
the world, protected by the threefold Veda, prospers and does not sink.

children.text: kṛṣipāśupālye vaṇijyā ca vārtā dhānyapaśuhiraṇyakupyaviṣṭipradānād aupakārikī ||
children.translated_text: Vārttā is agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; it is useful because it provides grain, cattle, gold, goods, and labor service.

children.text: tayā svapakṣaṃ parapakṣaṃ ca vaśīkaroti kośadaṇḍābhyām ||
children.translated_text: By means of it, through treasury and army, he brings both his own side and the enemy's side under control.

children.text: ānvīkṣikī trayī vārttānāṃ yogakṣemasādhano daṇḍaḥ tasya nītir daṇḍanītiḥ alabdhalābhārthā labdhaparirakṣaṇī rakṣitavivardhanī vṛddhasya tīrthe pratipādanī ca ||
children.translated_text: Daṇḍa (coercive power) is the means of acquisition and security for ānvīkṣikī, the threefold Veda, and vārttā; its policy is daṇḍanīti, which aims at gaining what has not been gained, protecting what has been gained, increasing what has been protected, and assigning what has increased to a worthy place.
On it the course of worldly life depends.
Therefore one who desires the course of worldly life should always keep the rod raised.

children.text: na hyevaṃvidhaṃ vaśopanayanam asti bhūtānāṃ yathā daṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: For there is no means of bringing beings under control like daṇḍa,
so the teachers say.
<s>Kauṭilya</s> says: no.
For a harsh punishment agitates beings.
A mild punishment is despised.
A punishment suited to what is deserved is respected.

children.text: suvijñātapraṇīto hi daṇḍaḥ prajā dharmārthakāmair yojayati ||
children.translated_text: For punishment, when well understood and properly applied, joins the subjects with dharma, artha, and kāma.

children.text: duṣpraṇītaḥ kāmakrodhābhyām avajñānād vā vānaprasthaparivrājakān api kopayati kimaṅga punar gṛhasthān ||
children.translated_text: When badly applied, through desire, anger, or contempt, it enrages even forest-dwellers and wandering ascetics, how much more householders.
But when it is not duly applied, it brings about <s>mātsyanyāya</s> (the law of the fishes).
For in the absence of one who bears <s>daṇḍa</s> (coercive authority), the stronger swallows the weaker.
Protected by it, one prospers.
The world of the four <s>varṇas</s> and <s>āśramas</s>, protected by the king with <s>daṇḍa</s>,
being devoted to the duties and acts proper to itself, proceeds on its own paths.
Therefore the three sciences have <s>daṇḍa</s> as their root.
<s>Daṇḍa</s>, rooted in discipline, brings acquisition and security to living beings.
Discipline is both acquired and natural.
For training shapes a receptive nature, not an unreceptive one.
Knowledge disciplines an intellect fixed on service, hearing, grasping, retention, understanding, reasoning for and against, and penetration to truth, not any other.

children.text: vidyānāṃ tu yathāsvam ācāryaprāmāṇyād vinayo niyamaśca ||
children.translated_text: For the sciences, discipline and rule come in each case from the authority of the teacher.
After the tonsure rite has been performed, he should apply himself to writing and arithmetic.

children.text: vṛttopanayanastrayīm ānvīkṣikīṃ ca śiṣṭebhyo vārttām adhyakṣebhyo daṇḍanītiṃ vaktṛprayoktṛbhyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: After initiation, he should learn the three Vedas and <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> (philosophical inquiry) from the learned, <s>vārttā</s> (economics) from superintendents, and <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (political discipline) from teachers and practitioners.
He should observe studentship until the sixteenth year.
After that come his beard-shaving rite and marriage.
There should be constant association with elders learned in the sciences for the increase of discipline, because discipline has that as its root.
In the first part of the day he should undergo training in the sciences of elephants, horses, chariots, and weapons;
in the latter part, in listening to <s>itihāsa</s> (traditional history).

children.text: purāṇam itivṛttam ākhyāyikodāharaṇaṃ dharmaśāstram arthaśāstraṃ cetītihāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Itihāsa</s> consists of <s>purāṇa</s>, accounts of events, tales, examples, <s>dharmaśāstra</s>, and <s>arthaśāstra</s>.

children.text: śeṣam ahorātrabhāgam apūrvagrahaṇaṃ gṛhītaparicayaṃ ca kuryāt agṛhītānām ābhīkṣṇyaśravaṇaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: During the remaining part of day and night he should learn what is new, review what has been learned, and repeatedly hear what has not been grasped.

children.text: śrutāddhi prajñopajāyate prajñāyā yogo yogād ātmavatteti vidyānāṃ sāmarthyam ||
children.translated_text: For from hearing arises insight, from insight application, and from application self-possession; this is the efficacy of the sciences.

children.text: vidyāvinīto rājā hi prajānāṃ vinaye rataḥ
children.translated_text: For a king disciplined by knowledge, devoted to the disciplining of his subjects,
enjoys the earth without rival, intent on the welfare of all beings.
Since learning is the cause of discipline, he should accomplish conquest of the senses by abandoning desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, and exhilaration.
Conquest of the senses is the non-deviation of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose in regard to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, or else the practice of the treatise.
For this whole treatise is concerned with conquest of the senses.

children.text: tadviruddhavṛttir avaśyendriyaś cāturanto api rājā sadyo vinaśyati ||
children.translated_text: A king whose conduct is opposed to that and whose senses are uncontrolled, even if he rules to the four ends of the earth, quickly perishes.

children.text: yathā dāṇḍakyo nāma bhojaḥ kāmād brāhmaṇakanyām abhimanyamānaḥ sabandhurāṣṭro vinanāśa karālaśca vaidehaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus <s>Dāṇḍakya</s>, a <s>Bhoja</s>, perished with his kinsmen and realm because through desire he coveted a Brahmin maiden, and so did <s>Karāla</s> the <s>Vaideha</s>.
Through anger, <s>Janamejaya</s>, attacking the Brahmins, perished, and so did <s>Tālajaṅgha</s> against the <s>Bhṛgus</s>.
Through greed, <s>Aila</s>, exacting too much from the four <s>varṇas</s>, perished, and so did <s>Ajabindu</s> the <s>Sauvīra</s>.

children.text: mānād rāvaṇaḥ paradārān aprayacchan duryodhano rājyād aṃśaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Through pride, <s>Rāvaṇa</s> perished because he would not return another's wife, and <s>Duryodhana</s> because he would not yield a share of the kingdom.
Through arrogance, <s>Dambhodbhava</s>, contemptuous of beings, perished, and so did <s>Arjuna</s> of the <s>Haihaya</s> line.

children.text: harṣād vātāpir agastyam atyāsādayan vṛṣṇisaṃghaśca dvaipāyanam iti ||
children.translated_text: Through exultation, <s>Vātāpi</s> perished by assailing <s>Agastya</s> too rashly, and the <s>Vṛṣṇi</s> confederacy by offending <s>Dvaipāyana</s>.

children.text: ete cānye ca bahavaḥ śatruṣaḍvargam āśritāḥ
children.translated_text: These and many other kings, resorting to the sixfold group of enemies,
uncontrolled in their senses, perished together with their kinsmen and realms.
Having cast off the sixfold group of enemies, <s>Jāmadagnya</s>, with conquered senses,
and <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, son of <s>Nābhāga</s>, enjoyed the earth for a long time.

children.text: tasmād ariṣaḍvargatyāgenendriyajayaṃ kurvīta vṛddhasaṃyogena prajñām cāreṇa cakṣuḥ utthānena yogakṣemasādhanam kāryānuśāsanena svadharmasthāpanam vinayaṃ vidyopadeśena lokapriyatvam arthasaṃyogena vṛttim ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, by abandoning the sixfold group of enemies, he should practice conquest of the senses; through association with elders, wisdom; through spies, sight; through energetic activity, the securing of acquisition and protection; through supervision of tasks, establishment in one's own <s>dharma</s>; through instruction in the sciences, discipline; and through connection with wealth, livelihood.

children.text: evaṃ vaśyendriyaḥ parastrīdravyahiṃsāśca varjayet svapnaṃ laulyam anṛtam uddhataveṣatvam anarthyasaṃyogam adharmasaṃyuktam anarthasaṃyuktaṃ ca vyavahāram ||
children.translated_text: Thus, with his senses under control, he should avoid others' wives, others' wealth, and violence, as well as sleep, fickleness, falsehood, haughty dress, association with harmful things, and conduct joined with <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness) and <s>anartha</s> (harm).

children.text: dharmārthāvirodhena kāmaṃ seveta na niḥsukhaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: He should enjoy <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) without conflict with <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>; he should not be without happiness.
Or he should pursue the <s>trivarga</s> (three aims) equally, each bound up with the others.

children.text: eko hyatyāsevito dharmārthakāmānām ātmānam itarau ca pīḍayati ||
children.translated_text: For any one of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s>, if pursued to excess, harms itself and the other two.
<s>Artha</s> alone is foremost, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.
For <s>dharma</s> and <s>kāma</s> have <s>artha</s> as their root.

children.text: maryādāṃ sthāpayed ācāryān amātyān vā ya enam apāyasthānebhyo vārayeyuḥ chāyānālikāpratodena vā rahasi pramādyantam abhitudeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: He should establish a restraining boundary in the form of teachers or ministers, who would keep him from places of danger, or privately prod him, when he is negligent, with the goad of the shadow-clock and water-clock.

children.text: sahāyasādhyaṃ rājatvaṃ cakram ekaṃ na vartate
children.translated_text: Kingship is accomplished with helpers; a single wheel does not turn.

children.text: kurvīta sacivāṃstasmāt teṣāṃ ca śṛṇuyān matam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore he should appoint counselors and listen to their opinion.
He should make his fellow students ministers, since their purity and capacity have been seen, says <s>Bhāradvāja</s>.
For they are trustworthy to him.
<s>Viśālākṣa</s> says that this is not so.
Because they have played with him, they treat him with contempt.

children.text: ye hyasya guhyasadharmāṇastān amātyān kurvīta samānaśīlavyasanatvāt ||
children.translated_text: He should make ministers of those who share his secrets, because their character and vices are the same as his.
For, from fear that he knows their vulnerable points, they do not offend against him.
This fault is common to both, say the <s>Pārāśaras</s>.
He too would have to follow their deeds and misdeeds out of fear that they know his vulnerable points.
To however many people the lord of men reveals a secret,

children.text: avaśaḥ karmaṇā tena vaśyo bhavati tāvatām ||
children.translated_text: by that act he becomes helpless and subject to that many.

children.text: yainam āpatsu prāṇābādhayuktāsvanugṛhṇīyustān amātyān kurvīta dṛṣṭānurāgatvāt iti ||
children.translated_text: He should make ministers of those who would aid him in calamities involving danger to life, because their affection has been seen.
<s>Piśuna</s> says that this is not so.
That is devotion, not a quality of intelligence.

children.text: saṃkhyātārtheṣu karmasu niyuktā ye yathādiṣṭam arthaṃ saviśeṣaṃ vā kuryustān amātyān kurvīta dṛṣṭaguṇatvāt iti ||
children.translated_text: Those who, when appointed to tasks with measurable results, perform the task exactly as ordered, or even with distinction, he should make <s>amātyas</s> (ministers), because their qualities have been seen, so it is said.
Not so, says <s>Kauṇapadanta</s>.
For these men are not endowed with the other qualities of ministers.
He should make hereditary ministers, those whose fathers and grandfathers served as ministers, because their services have been seen.

children.text: te hyenam apacarantam api na tyajanti sagandhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For even when he behaves wrongly, they do not abandon him, since they are of the same stock.
This is seen even among non-human creatures.

children.text: gāvo hyasagandhaṃ gogaṇam atikramya sagandheṣvevāvatiṣṭhante iti ||
children.translated_text: For cows pass by a herd of cattle that is not of their own scent and remain only among those of their own scent, so it is said.
Not so, says <s>Vātavyādhi</s>.

children.text: te hyasya sarvam avagṛhya svāmivat pracaranti ||
children.translated_text: For they seize all that belongs to him and behave like masters.
Therefore he should make new men, skilled in policy, his ministers.

children.text: navāstu yamasthāne daṇḍadharaṃ manyamānā nāparādhyanti iti ||
children.translated_text: New men, thinking of the wielder of punishment as standing in the place of <s>Yama</s>, do not commit offenses, so it is said.
Not so, says <s>Bāhudantīputra</s>.
A man who knows the treatise but has no experience of action may become dejected in practical affairs.

children.text: tasmād abhijanaprajñāśaucaśauryānurāgayuktān amātyān kurvīta guṇaprādhānyāt iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore he should make ministers who are endowed with noble birth, intelligence, purity, courage, and loyalty, because qualities are the chief consideration, so it is said.
All of this is appropriate, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.
For a man’s capability is inferred from the capability shown in the work.

children.text: sāmarthyataśca vibhajyāmātyavibhavaṃ deśakālau ca karma ca
children.translated_text: And according to capability, after apportioning the resources of the ministers, the place and time, and the work,

children.text: amātyāḥ sarva evaite kāryāḥ syur na tu mantriṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: all these should indeed be made <s>amātyas</s> (ministers), but not <s>mantrins</s> (counselors).

children.text: jānapado 'bhijātaḥ svavagrahaḥ kṛtaśilpaścakṣuṣmān prājño dhārayiṣṇur dakṣo vāgmī pragalbhaḥ pratipattimān utsāhaprabhāvayuktaḥ kleśasahaḥ śucir maitro dṛḍhabhaktiḥ śīlabalārogyasattvayuktaḥ stambhacāpalahīnaḥ sampriyo vairāṇām akartetyamātyasampat ||
children.translated_text: The excellence of an <s>amātya</s> is this: he is native to the country, of noble birth, possessed of his own standing, trained in skills, clear-sighted, intelligent, retentive, competent, eloquent, bold, ready-witted, endowed with energy and influence, able to endure hardship, pure, friendly, firmly devoted, endowed with character, strength, health, and vitality, free from rigidity and fickleness, agreeable, and not a maker of enemies.
Of these, those lacking a quarter or a half of the qualities are middling and inferior respectively.

children.text: teṣāṃ janapadabhijanam avagrahaṃ cāptataḥ parīkṣeta samānavidyebhyaḥ śilpaṃ śāstracakṣuṣmattāṃ ca karmārambheṣu prajñāṃ dhārayiṣṇutāṃ dākṣyaṃ ca kathāyogeṣu vāgmitvaṃ prāgalbhyaṃ pratibhānavattvaṃ ca saṃvāsibhyaḥ śīlabalārogyasattvayogam astambham acāpalaṃ ca pratyakṣataḥ sampriyatvam avairatvaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Among them he should examine, from trustworthy persons, their native district, noble birth, and personal standing; from fellow students, their skill, knowledge of treatise, and clear-sightedness; in the undertaking of works, their intelligence, retentiveness, and competence; in conversation, their eloquence, boldness, and presence of mind; from those who live with them, their possession of character, strength, health, and vitality, and their freedom from rigidity and fickleness; and directly, their agreeableness and absence of hostility.
For royal activity is known by direct perception, by indirect report, and by inference.
What is seen by oneself is direct perception.
What is reported by another is indirect knowledge.
Inspection of what has been done and not done in undertakings is inference.

children.text: yaugapadyāt tu karmaṇām anekatvād anekasthatvācca deśakālātyayo mā bhūd iti parokṣam amātyaiḥ kārayedityamātyakarma ||
children.translated_text: But because works are simultaneous, numerous, and located in many places, he should have indirect matters carried out by ministers, so that place and time may not be lost; this is the work of ministers.

children.text: purohitam uditoditakulaśīlaṃ sāṅge vede daive nimitte daṇḍanītyāṃ cābhivinītam āpadāṃ daivamānuṣīṇām atharvabhir upāyaiśca pratikartāraṃ kurvīta ||
children.translated_text: He should appoint as <s>purohita</s> (chaplain) a man of eminent family and character, thoroughly trained in the Veda with its auxiliaries, in divine signs and omens, and in <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (the science of rule), and able to counteract divine and human calamities by Atharvan rites and other means.

children.text: tam ācāryaṃ śiṣyaḥ pitaraṃ putro bhṛtyaḥ svāminam iva cānuvarteta ||
children.translated_text: He should follow him as a pupil follows a teacher, a son his father, and a servant his master.
Kingly power, strengthened by a Brahmin and consecrated by the counsel of ministers,
conquers what has not been conquered, completely, armed by conformity to the treatise.
With a minister and a <s>purohita</s> as companions, after placing the ministers in ordinary offices, he should test them by secret trials.
The king should disgrace the <s>purohita</s>, pretending not to tolerate that he has been engaged in officiating for unfit sacrificers and in teaching them.

children.text: sa sattribhiḥ śapathapūrvam ekaikam amātyam upajāpayet adhārmiko 'yaṃ rājā sādhu dhārmikam anyam asya tatkulīnam aparuddhaṃ kulyam ekapragrahaṃ sāmantam āṭavikam aupapādikaṃ vā pratipādayāmaḥ sarveṣām etad rocate kathaṃ vā tava iti ||
children.translated_text: He, through secret agents, should incite each minister individually after an oath: 'This king is unrighteous. Good, let us install in his place another righteous man: one of his family, an excluded kinsman of the line, one with a single following, a neighboring lord, a forest chief, or an adventitious claimant. This is pleasing to everyone; what about you?'
If he refuses, he is pure.
This is the test by <s>dharma</s> (righteousness).

children.text: senāpatir asatpragraheṇāvakṣiptaḥ sattribhir ekaikam amātyam upajāpayet lobhanīyenārthena rājavināśāya sarveṣām etad rocate kathaṃ vā tava iti ||
children.translated_text: The commander of the army, disgraced on account of taking up improper men, should have secret agents incite each minister individually with tempting wealth for the destruction of the king: 'This is pleasing to everyone; what about you?'
If he refuses, he is pure.
This is the test by <s>artha</s> (wealth).

children.text: parivrājikā labdhaviśvāsāntaḥpure kṛtasatkārā mahāmātram ekaikam upajapet rājamahiṣī tvāṃ kāmayate kṛtasamāgamopāyā mahān arthaśca te bhaviṣyati iti ||
children.translated_text: A female ascetic who has gained confidence in the inner apartments and has been honored there should entice each high official individually: 'The chief queen desires you; the means for a meeting have been arranged, and great wealth will come to you.'
If he refuses, he is pure.
This is the test by <s>kāma</s> (desire).
On the pretext of a festive gathering, one minister should summon all the ministers.
Because of that alarm, the king should confine them.

children.text: kāpaṭikaścātra pūrvāvaruddhasteṣām arthamānāvakṣiptam ekaikam amātyam upajapet asatpravṛtto 'yaṃ rājā sādhvenaṃ hatvānyaṃ pratipādayāmaḥ sarveṣām etad rocate kathaṃ vā tava iti ||
children.translated_text: Then a deceitful agent, previously imprisoned, should incite each minister, whose wealth and honor have been diminished for their sake: 'This king has entered upon evil conduct. Good, after killing him, let us install another. This is pleasing to everyone; what about you?'
If he refuses, he is pure.
This is the test by fear.

children.text: tatra dharmopadhāśuddhān dharmasthīyakaṇṭakaśodhaneṣu karmasu sthāpayet arthopadhāśuddhān samāhartṛsaṃnidhātṛnicayakarmasu kāmopadhāśuddhān bāhyābhyantaravihārarakṣāsu bhayopadhāśuddhān āsannakāryeṣu rājñaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, he should place those purified by the <s>dharma</s>-test in judicial and crime-suppression duties; those purified by the wealth-test in the duties of collector, treasurer, and stores; those purified by the desire-test in guarding external and internal pleasures; and those purified by the fear-test in the king's immediate affairs.
He should make those purified by all the tests his counselors.
Those impure in every respect he should employ in mines, material stores, elephant forests, and workshops.
Ministers purified with respect to the three aims and fear, in their own duties...
The teachers are agreed that he should appoint them according to purity.

children.text: na tveva kuryād ātmānaṃ devīṃ vā lakṣyam īśvaraḥ
children.translated_text: But the ruler should never make himself, or the queen, the target of a test.
For testing the purity of ministers, this is the view of <s>Kauṭilya</s>.
One should not corrupt a person who is uncorrupted, as water is corrupted by poison.
For if he has once become corrupt, the remedy may sometimes not be found.
And a mind made turbid by the four kinds of upadhā (secret test),
once fixed in the resolve of strong men, would not turn back before reaching the end.

children.text: tasmād bāhyam adhiṣṭhānaṃ kṛtvā kārye caturvidhe
children.translated_text: Therefore, having made an external basis for the fourfold business,
the king should investigate the purity and impurity of ministers by means of sattrins (secret agents).

When the class of ministers has been purified by the upadhās, he should produce secret agents: those in the guises of kāpaṭika, udāsthita, gṛhapatika, vaidehaka, and tāpasa, and also sattrins, tīkṣṇas, rasadas, and begging women.
A bold student who knows the vulnerable points of others is a kāpaṭika.

children.text: tam arthamānābhyāṃ protsāhya mantrī brūyāt rājānaṃ māṃ ca pramāṇaṃ kṛtvā yasya yad akuśalaṃ paśyasi tat tadānīm eva pratyādiśa iti ||
children.translated_text: After encouraging him with wealth and honor, the minister should say, "Taking the king and me as authority, whatever misconduct you see in anyone, report it at that very time."
One who has fallen back from renunciation, and is endowed with intelligence and purity, is an udāsthita.

children.text: sa vārttākarmapradiṣṭāyāṃ bhūmau prabhūtahiraṇyāntevāsī karma kārayet ||
children.translated_text: On land assigned for productive enterprise, with many pupils and abundant money, he should have work carried out.
From the fruit of that work he should provide food, clothing, and lodging for all renunciants.

children.text: vṛttikāmāṃścopajapet etenaiva veṣeṇa rājārthaścaritavyo bhaktavetanakāle copasthātavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: He should secretly recruit those who desire a livelihood, saying, "In this very guise the king's business is to be carried out, and at the time of food and wages you must present yourselves."

children.text: sarvapravrajitāśca svaṃ svaṃ vargam evam upajapeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: And all renunciants should in this way secretly recruit their own group.
A farmer whose livelihood is exhausted, and who is endowed with intelligence and purity, is one in the gṛhapatika guise.

children.text: sa kṛṣikarmapradiṣṭāyāṃ bhūmau iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa ||
children.translated_text: On land assigned for agricultural work, the same procedure applies as in the preceding case.
A merchant whose livelihood is exhausted, and who is endowed with intelligence and purity, is one in the vaidehaka guise.

children.text: sa vaṇikkarmapradiṣṭāyāṃ bhūmau iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa ||
children.translated_text: On land assigned for mercantile work, the same procedure applies as in the preceding case.
A shaven-headed or matted-haired man who desires a livelihood is one in the tāpasa guise.

children.text: sa nagarābhyāśe prabhūtamuṇḍajaṭilāntevāsī śākaṃ yavamuṣṭiṃ vā māsadvimāsāntaraṃ prakāśam aśnīyāt gūḍham iṣṭam āhāram ||
children.translated_text: Near the city, with many shaven-headed and matted-haired pupils, he should openly eat greens or a handful of barley at intervals of one or two months, while secretly eating whatever food he likes.
The pupils in the vaidehaka guise should honor him with displays of occult success.
And his pupils should proclaim, "That man is a siddha, possessed of occult efficacy."

children.text: samedhāśāstibhiścābhigatānām aṅgavidyayā śiṣyasaṃjñābhiśca karmāṇyabhijane avasitānyādiśet alpalābham agnidāhaṃ corabhayaṃ dūṣyavadhaṃ tuṣṭidānaṃ videśapravṛttijñānam idam adya śvo vā bhaviṣyati idaṃ vā rājā kariṣyati iti ||
children.translated_text: By predictions of such success, by physiognomy, and by signs from his pupils, he should announce to visitors actions that have been ascertained among prominent families: a small gain, a fire, danger from thieves, the killing of a disaffected person, a gift for appeasement, knowledge of activity abroad, "This will happen today or tomorrow," or "The king will do this."
His hidden agents and sattrins should bring that about for him.
For those endowed with courage, intelligence, and force of speech, he should declare royal fortune and speak of connection with a minister.
And the minister should provide for them by livelihood and work.

children.text: ye ca kāraṇād abhikruddhāstān arthamānābhyāṃ śamayet akāraṇakruddhāṃstūṣṇīṃ daṇḍena rājadviṣṭakāriṇaśca ||
children.translated_text: Those who are angry for a reason he should pacify with wealth and honor; those angry without reason, and those who do what the king hates, he should quietly deal with by punishment.
Honored by the king with wealth and honor among those who live from the king,
they should learn purity; these are proclaimed to be the five institutions.

children.text: ye cāpyasaṃbandhino 'vaśyabhartavyāste lakṣaṇam aṅgavidyāṃ jambhakavidyāṃ māyāgatam āśramadharmaṃ nimittam antaracakram ityadhīyānāḥ sattriṇaḥ saṃsargavidyāṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Those also who have no close ties and must be maintained, studying marks, physiognomy, jambhaka magic, illusion, the duties of religious orders, omens, inner-circle lore, and the science of association, are sattrins.

children.text: ye janapade śūrāstyaktātmāno hastinaṃ vyālaṃ vā dravyahetoḥ pratiyodhayeyuste tīkṣṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those in the countryside who are brave, who have thrown away concern for their lives, and who would fight an elephant or a wild beast for the sake of money, are tīkṣṇas.

children.text: ye bandhuṣu niḥsnehāḥ krūrā alasāśca te rasadāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those who have no affection for their relatives, and are cruel and idle, are rasadas.

children.text: parivrājikā vṛttikāmā daridrā vidhavā pragalbhā brāhmaṇyantaḥpure kṛtasatkārā mahāmātrakulānyabhigacchet ||
children.translated_text: A female wandering ascetic who desires a livelihood, poor, widowed, bold, a Brāhmaṇī honored in the inner palace, should visit the households of high officials.
By this, shaven-headed women and low-born women are also explained.

children.text: tān rājā svaviṣaye mantripurohitasenāpatiyuvarājadauvārikāntarvaṃśikapraśāstṛsamāhartṛsaṃnidhātṛpradeṣṭṛnāyakapauravyāvahārikakārmāntikamantripariṣadadhyakṣadaṇḍadurgāntapālāṭavikeṣu śraddheyadeśaveṣaśilpabhāṣābhijanāpadeśān bhaktitaḥ sāmarthyayogāccāpasarpayet ||
children.translated_text: In his own realm the king should infiltrate them, according to loyalty and fitness of capacity, among the minister, chaplain, commander, crown prince, doorkeeper, inner-chamber officer, administrator, collector-general, treasurer, district officer, military leader, city officer, judge, superintendent of works, council of ministers, superintendents, the army, forts, frontier guards, and forest chiefs, using credible pretexts of region, dress, craft, speech, lineage, and locality.
Tīkṣṇas serving as holders of umbrellas, pitchers, fans, sandals, seats, conveyances, mounts, and accessories should learn their external movements.
The sattrins should deliver that information to the institutions.

Cooks, kitchen servants, bathers, masseurs, bed-spreaders, barbers, adorners, water attendants, rasadas, and those disguised as hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, mutes, deaf persons, dullards, and blind persons, as well as actors, dancers, singers, musicians, speakers by profession, performers, and women, should learn their internal movements.
The begging women should deliver that information to the institutions.
The pupils of the institutions should carry out the transmission of intelligence by signs and writing.
And the institutions, or those agents, should not know one another.

children.text: bhikṣukīpratiṣedhe dvāḥsthaparamparā mātāpitṛvyañjanāḥ śilpakārikāḥ kuśīlavā dāsyo vā gītapāṭhyavādyabhāṇḍagūḍhalekhyasaṃjñābhir vā cāraṃ nirhareyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: When begging women are barred, a chain of doorkeepers, agents disguised as mothers or fathers, craftswomen, performers, female slaves, or secret writings and signs in the apparatus of singing, recitation, and music should carry the intelligence out.
Or a secret departure may be made by means of chronic illness, madness, fire, or the discharge of poison.
When the three give a single statement, there is assurance.
But when they repeatedly fail, silent punishment is the restraint.
The secret agents mentioned in the removal of thorns should live among enemies, paid by them, and, not coming into contact with one another, for the sake of espionage.
They are to be double-paid agents.
And he should make double-paid agents of those whose sons and wives have been taken.

children.text: tāṃścāriprahitān vidyāt teṣāṃ śaucaṃ ca tadvidhaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: He should know those who have been sent by the enemy, and test their purity by men of the same kind.

children.text: evaṃ śatrau ca mitre ca madhyame cāvapeccarān
children.translated_text: In this way he should plant spies in an enemy, in an ally, and in the middle king,
and in the neutral king, and also in all eighteen official posts of those kings.
Their internal household spies should be hunchbacks, dwarfs, and eunuchs,
women skilled in crafts, mutes, and various people of foreign birth.
In forts, merchants should be stationary agents; at the borders of forts, accomplished ascetics;
in the countryside, farmers and secluded householders; at the borders of the realm, herdsmen;
in the forest, forest-dwellers, ascetics, foresters, and the like should be appointed,
for the purpose of knowing another's activity; and there should be swift chains of spies.
These same agents of another ruler are to be detected by agents of just the same kinds.
Stationary agents who move among spies are hidden and designated as not hidden.
In order to know the enemy's secret agents, he should station chief men on the frontiers, men shown by practical causes to be disaffected but on the side of those fit for action.
He should station them on the borders for the purpose of knowing the enemy's secret agents.
Having created secret agents among high officials, he should set secret agents upon the townspeople and country people.
Ascetic agents and disputants should start a quarrel in gatherings of officials, assemblies, guilds, and common people.

children.text: sarvaguṇasampannaścāyaṃ rājā śrūyate na cāsya kaścid guṇo dṛśyate yaḥ paurajānapadān daṇḍakarābhyāṃ pīḍayati iti ||
children.translated_text: They should say: 'This king is heard to possess every virtue, but no virtue of his is seen, since he oppresses the townspeople and country people with punishment and taxes.'
There, those who approve the statement should be opposed by the other agent, and he should oppose that statement as well.

children.text: mātsyanyāyābhibhūtāḥ prajā manuṃ vaivasvataṃ rājānaṃ cakrire ||
children.translated_text: The people, overwhelmed by <s>mātsyanyāya</s> (the law of the fish), made <s>Manu Vaivasvata</s> king.

children.text: dhānyaṣaḍbhāgaṃ paṇyadaśabhāgaṃ hiraṇyaṃ cāsya bhāgadheyaṃ prakalpayāmāsuḥ ||
children.translated_text: They assigned to him as his share one-sixth of the grain, one-tenth of merchandise, and gold.
Maintained by that, kings bring acquisition and security to their subjects.
Those who do not pay punishment and taxes take upon themselves the sin of kings when they fail to bring acquisition and security to the people.

children.text: tasmād uñchaṣaḍbhāgam āraṇyakāpi nirvapanti tasyaitad bhāgadheyaṃ yo 'smān gopāyati iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore even forest ascetics set aside one-sixth of what they glean, saying, 'This is the share of him who protects us.'
This is the station of <s>Indra</s> and <s>Yama</s>; kings visibly show wrath and favor.
Even divine punishment touches those who despise them.
Therefore kings must not be despised.
In this way he should restrain the petty people.
And they should find out the rumor.

children.text: ye cāsya dhānyapaśuhiraṇyānyājīvanti tair upakurvanti vyasane 'bhyudaye vā kupitaṃ bandhuṃ rāṣṭraṃ vā vyāvartayanti amitram āṭavikaṃ vā pratiṣedhayanti teṣāṃ muṇḍajaṭilavyañjanāstuṣṭātuṣṭatvaṃ vidyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those who live on his grain, cattle, and gold, who assist him in calamity or prosperity, who turn back an angry kinsman or the realm, or who ward off an enemy or a forest chieftain: among them, agents disguised as shaven ascetics and matted-hair ascetics should find out who is satisfied and who is dissatisfied.
He should honor the satisfied still further with wealth and respect.
He should conciliate the dissatisfied, for the sake of satisfaction, by concession and by conciliation.
Or he should split them from one another, and from neighboring chiefs, forest chiefs, men of their own family, and those who are confined.
If they are still dissatisfied, he should make them incur the hatred of the countryside by placing them in charge of collecting punishments and taxes.
When they are hated, he should deal with them by secret punishment or through the anger of the countryside.

children.text: guptaputradārān ākarakarmānteṣu vā vāsayet pareṣām āspadabhayāt ||
children.translated_text: Or he should settle them, with their sons and wives kept under guard, in mines and factories, because of the danger that they may become a base for enemies.
The angry, the greedy, the fearful, and the proud are persons fit for action by enemies.

children.text: teṣāṃ kārtāntikanaimittikamauhūrtikavyañjanāḥ parasparābhisambandham amitrāṭavikasambandhaṃ vā vidyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among them, agents disguised as astrologers, omen-readers, and hour-diviners should find out their mutual connections, or their connection with an enemy or forest chieftain.
He should honor the satisfied with wealth and respect.
He should deal with the dissatisfied by conciliation, gifts, division, and punishment.
Thus, in his own domain, a discerning ruler should protect
both chief men and petty men, whether fit or unfit for action, from incitement by another.
The winning over of those fit and unfit for action in one's own domain has been explained; it should now be stated for the enemy's domain.

children.text: saṃśrutyārthān vipralabdhaḥ tulyakāriṇoḥ śilpe vopakāre vā vimānitaḥ vallabhāvaruddhaḥ samāhūya parājitaḥ pravāsopataptaḥ kṛtvā vyayam alabdhakāryaḥ svadharmād dāyādyād voparuddhaḥ mānādhikārābhyāṃ bhraṣṭaḥ kulyair antarhitaḥ prasabhābhimṛṣṭastrīkaḥ kārābhinyastaḥ paroktadaṇḍitaḥ mithyācāravāritaḥ sarvasvam āhāritaḥ bandhanaparikliṣṭaḥ pravāsitabandhuḥ iti kruddhavargaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The class of the angry consists of one who has been deceived after an agreement on goods, one who has been humiliated when equal in work, craft, or service, one obstructed by a favorite, one summoned and defeated, one afflicted by exile, one who incurred expense and did not obtain his object, one blocked from his own <s>dharma</s> or inheritance, one fallen from honor and office, one excluded by his kinsmen, one whose wife has been forcibly violated, one thrown into prison, one punished because of another's word, one prevented from false conduct, one whose entire property has been taken, one distressed by bonds, and one whose kinsman has been exiled.

children.text: svayam upahataḥ viprakṛtaḥ pāpakarmābhikhyātaḥ tulyadoṣadaṇḍenodvignaḥ paryāttabhūmiḥ daṇḍenopanataḥ sarvādhikaraṇasthaḥ sahasopacitārthaḥ tatkulīno vāśaṃsuḥ pradviṣṭo rājñā rājadveṣī ca iti bhītavargaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The class of the fearful consists of one injured by himself, one wronged, one known for evil action, one agitated by a punishment equal to his offense, one whose land has been seized, one brought under control by punishment, one placed in all administrative offices, one who has suddenly amassed wealth, one born in that family and hoping for power, one hated by the king, and one who hates the king.

children.text: parikṣīṇaḥ anyāttasvaḥ kadaryaḥ vyasanī atyāhitavyavahāraśca iti lubdhavargaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The class of the greedy consists of one who is ruined, one whose property has been taken by another, a miser, an addict, and one engaged in extremely risky dealings.

children.text: ātmasaṃbhāvitaḥ mānakāmaḥ śatrupūjāmarṣitaḥ nīcair upahitaḥ tīkṣṇaḥ sāhasikaḥ bhogenāsaṃtuṣṭaḥ iti mānivargaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The class of the proud consists of one who thinks highly of himself, one who desires honor, one angered by honor shown to an enemy, one treated as inferior, one sharp-tempered, one reckless, and one not satisfied with enjoyment.

children.text: teṣāṃ muṇḍajaṭilavyañjanair yo yadbhaktiḥ kṛtyapakṣīyastaṃ tenopajāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Among them, through agents disguised as shaven ascetics and matted-hair ascetics, he should incite each man who is devoted to whatever side and is fit for action, by means suited to that man.

children.text: yathā madāndho hastī mattenādhiṣṭhito yad yad āsādayati tat sarvaṃ pramṛdnāti evam ayam aśāstracakṣur andho rājā paurajānapadavadhāyābhyutthitaḥ śakyam asya pratihastiprotsāhanenāpakartum amarṣaḥ kriyatām iti kruddhavargam upajāpayet ||
children.translated_text: As a rut-blind elephant, mounted by a drunken rider, tramples down whatever it comes upon, so this king, blind because the treatise is not his eye, has risen up for the slaughter of townsmen and country people. It is possible to injure him by stirring up a counter-elephant; let indignation be aroused. Thus he should incite the angry faction.

children.text: yathā līnaḥ sarpo yasmād bhayaṃ paśyati tatra viṣam utsṛjati evam ayaṃ rājā jātadoṣāśaṅkastvayi purā krodhaviṣam utsṛjati anyatra gamyatām iti bhītavargam upajāpayet ||
children.translated_text: As a hidden snake releases poison where it sees danger, so this king, suspecting that a fault has arisen in you, may soon release the poison of anger against you. Go elsewhere. Thus he should incite the fearful faction.

children.text: yathā śvagaṇināṃ dhenuḥ śvabhyo duhyate na brāhmaṇebhyaḥ evam ayaṃ rājā sattvaprajñāvākyaśaktihīnebhyo duhyate nātmaguṇasampannebhyaḥ asau rājā puruṣaviśeṣajñaḥ tatra gamyatām iti lubdhavargam upajāpayet ||
children.translated_text: As the cow of dog-keepers is milked for dogs and not for Brahmins, so this king is milked for men lacking strength, intelligence, and power of speech, not for those endowed with personal qualities. That king recognizes exceptional men; go there. Thus he should incite the greedy faction.

children.text: yathā caṇḍālodapānaścaṇḍālānām evopabhogyo nānyeṣām evam ayaṃ rājā nīco nīcānām evopabhogyo na tvadvidhānām āryāṇām asau rājā puruṣaviśeṣajñaḥ tatra gamyatām iti mānivargam upajāpayet ||
children.translated_text: As a well of <s>Caṇḍālas</s> is fit for the use of <s>Caṇḍālas</s> alone and not of others, so this low king is fit for low men alone, not for noble men such as you. That king recognizes exceptional men; go there. Thus he should incite the proud faction.
When they have accepted this, saying, 'So be it,' and have been bound together by paid service,
he should employ them, along with secret agents, according to their capacity, each in his own tasks.
In enemy territories he should win over those fit for subversion by conciliation and gifts,
and those not fit for subversion by dissension and force, while pointing out the enemy's faults.
After securing support on his own side and on the enemy's side, he should consider the undertaking of operations.
All undertakings must be preceded by <s>mantra</s> (secret counsel).

children.text: taduddeśaḥ saṃvṛtaḥ kathānām aniḥśrāvī pakṣibhir apyanālokyaḥ syāt
children.translated_text: The place for that counsel should be concealed, not letting conversations be overheard, and not visible even to birds.

children.text: śrūyate hi śukasārikābhir mantro bhinnaḥ śvabhir apyanyaiśca tiryagyonibhir iti ||
children.translated_text: For it is heard that counsel has been betrayed by parrots and mynah birds, even by dogs and other animals.
Therefore one who is not appointed should not approach the place of counsel.
One who breaks counsel should be destroyed.
For disclosure of counsel among envoys, ministers, and the lord occurs through hints and outward signs.
A hint is conduct different from the usual.
An outward sign is the taking in of a person's visible expression.

children.text: tasya saṃvaraṇam āyuktapuruṣarakṣaṇam ā kāryakālād iti ||
children.translated_text: The concealment of it consists in guarding the appointed persons until the time for action.

children.text: teṣāṃ hi pramādamadasuptapralāpāḥ kāmādir utsekaḥ pracchanno 'vamato vā mantraṃ bhinatti ||
children.translated_text: For among them, talk from carelessness, intoxication, or sleep, excitement beginning with desire, or a hidden or slighted person, breaks counsel.
Therefore he should guard counsel.
For disclosure of counsel brings loss of acquisition and security to the king and also to the persons appointed to that business.

children.text: tasmād guhyam eko mantrayeta iti bhāradvājaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore one should deliberate on a secret matter alone, says <s>Bhāradvāja</s>.

children.text: mantriṇām api hi mantriṇo bhavanti teṣām apyanye ||
children.translated_text: For even counselors have counselors, and those too have others.
This very succession of counselors breaks counsel.

children.text: tasmān nāsya pare vidyuḥ karma kiṃciccikīrṣitam
children.translated_text: Therefore others should not know any action that he intends to undertake;

children.text: ārabdhārastu jānīyur ārabdhaṃ kṛtam eva vā ||
children.translated_text: they should know the matter only after it has been begun, or after it has been completed.
There is no success of counsel for a single person, says <s>Viśālākṣa</s>.
For royal activity is known by direct perception, by indirect knowledge, and by inference.

children.text: anupalabdhasya jñānam upalabdhasya niścitabalādhānam arthadvaidhasya saṃśayacchedanam ekadeśadṛṣṭasya śeṣopalabdhir iti mantrisādhyam etat ||
children.translated_text: Knowledge of what has not been perceived, firm determination about what has been perceived, cutting off doubt when a matter has two aspects, and apprehending the remainder of what has been seen only in part: this is to be accomplished by counselors.
Therefore he should sit in counsel together with men mature in intelligence.

children.text: na kaṃcid avamanyeta sarvasya śṛṇuyān matam
children.translated_text: He should not despise anyone; he should listen to everyone's opinion.
A wise man should make use even of a child's meaningful speech.

children.text: etan mantrajñānam naitan mantrarakṣaṇam iti pārāśarāḥ ||
children.translated_text: This is knowledge of counsel; it is not protection of counsel, say the <s>Pārāśaras</s>.

children.text: yad asya kāryam abhipretaṃ tatpratirūpakaṃ mantriṇaḥ pṛcchet kāryam idam evam āsīt evaṃ vā yadi bhavet tat kathaṃ kartavyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Concerning the business he intends, he should ask the counselors about a corresponding semblance of it: 'This matter was so, or, if it were so, how should it be done?'
He should do as they say.
In this way there is both acquisition of counsel and concealment, so they say.
Not so, says <s>Piśuna</s>.

children.text: mantriṇo hi vyavahitam arthaṃ vṛttam avṛttaṃ vā pṛṣṭā anādareṇa bruvanti prakāśayanti vā ||
children.translated_text: For counselors, when asked about an indirect matter, whether it has happened or not, speak carelessly or disclose it.
That is a fault.

children.text: tasmāt karmasu ye yeṣvabhipretāstaiḥ saha mantrayeta ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, in particular works, he should deliberate with the very persons intended for those works.

children.text: tair mantrayamāṇo hi mantrasiddhiṃ guptiṃ ca labhate iti ||
children.translated_text: For by deliberating with them he obtains success in counsel and secrecy, so he says.
Not so, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.
For this has no fixed limit.
He should deliberate with three or four counselors.
For when deliberating with one alone, he does not reach a decision in difficult matters.
And a single counselor acts as he wishes, without restraint.

children.text: dvābhyāṃ mantrayamāṇo dvābhyāṃ saṃhatābhyām avagṛhyate vigṛhītābhyāṃ vināśyate ||
children.translated_text: When he deliberates with two, he is overpowered by the two if they are united, and ruined by them if they are divided.
Among three or four, that occurs only with difficulty.
But if it does occur, it becomes a great fault.

children.text: tataḥ pareṣu kṛcchreṇārthaniścayo gamyate mantro vā rakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: With more than that, the decision of the matter is reached only with difficulty, or the counsel is protected only with difficulty.

children.text: deśakālakāryavaśena tvekena saha dvābhyām eko vā yathāsāmarthyaṃ mantrayeta ||
children.translated_text: But according to place, time, and business, he should deliberate with one, with two, or alone, according to his capacity.

children.text: karmaṇām ārambhopāyaḥ puruṣadravyasampad deśakālavibhāgo vinipātapratīkāraḥ kāryasiddhir iti pañcāṅgo mantraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The means for beginning undertakings, the sufficiency of men and materials, the division of place and time, the counteraction of calamity, and the accomplishment of the work: these are the five limbs of counsel.
He should question them about these one by one and also collectively.
And from their reasons he should know the distinctions in their thinking.
When the objective has been obtained, he should not let the time pass by.

children.text: na dīrghakālaṃ mantrayeta na teṣāṃ pakṣīyair yeṣām apakuryāt ||
children.translated_text: He should not deliberate for a long time, nor with the partisans of those whom he would injure.
The <s>Mānavas</s> say that he should make a <s>mantripariṣad</s> (council of ministers) of twelve <s>amātyas</s> (ministers).
The followers of <s>Bṛhaspati</s> say sixteen.
The followers of <s>Uśanas</s> say twenty.
According to capacity, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.

children.text: te hyasya svapakṣaṃ parapakṣaṃ ca cintayeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: For they should deliberate on his own side and on the enemy's side.

children.text: akṛtārambham ārabdhānuṣṭhānam anuṣṭhitaviśeṣaṃ niyogasampadaṃ ca karmaṇāṃ kuryuḥ ||
children.translated_text: In undertakings, they should bring about the initiation of what has not been begun, the carrying forward of what has been begun, the special improvement of what has been carried out, and the success of assignments.
He should examine affairs together with those who are nearby.
With those who are not nearby he should deliberate by sending letters.
For <s>Indra</s>'s council of minister-sages numbers a thousand.
That is his eye.
Therefore they call this two-eyed man thousand-eyed.

children.text: ātyayike kārye mantriṇo mantripariṣadaṃ cāhūya brūyāt ||
children.translated_text: In an urgent matter he should summon the ministers and the council of ministers and state it.

children.text: tatra yadbhūyiṣṭhā brūyuḥ kāryasiddhikaraṃ vā tat kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: There he should do what the majority say, or what brings about success in the matter.
And while acting,

children.text: nāsya guhyaṃ pare vidyuśchidraṃ vidyāt parasya ca
children.translated_text: others should not know his secret, and he should know the weak point of the enemy;

children.text: gūhet kūrmevāṅgāni yat syād vivṛtam ātmanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: he should hide whatever of himself is exposed, like a tortoise its limbs.

children.text: yathā hyaśrotriyaḥ śrāddhaṃ na satāṃ bhoktum arhati
children.translated_text: For just as one who has not studied the Veda is not fit to eat the <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral offering) of good men,

children.text: evam aśrutaśāstrārtho na mantraṃ śrotum arhati ||
children.translated_text: so one who has not learned the meaning of the treatise is not fit to hear counsel.
When the counsel has been settled, there is the appointment of an envoy.
One endowed with the qualities of a minister is an envoy with unrestricted authority.
One lacking a quarter of the qualities has a limited commission.
One lacking half the qualities is a bearer of the royal message.
He should set out with vehicles, mounts, men, and provisions well arranged.

children.text: śāsanam evaṃ vācyaḥ paraḥ sa vakṣyatyevam tasyedaṃ prativākyam evam atisaṃdhātavyam ityadhīyāno gacchet ||
children.translated_text: He should go after rehearsing: 'The other ruler is to be addressed thus; he will answer thus; this is the reply to him; thus he is to be outmaneuvered.'
He should also enter into contact with forest chiefs, frontier guards, and the leading men of towns and districts.
He should inspect, for himself and for the enemy, the grounds for army stations, battle, defense, and retreat.
He should ascertain the size of the fortress and country, and their resources, means of subsistence, protections, and weak points.
He should enter the enemy's seat only when permitted.

children.text: śāsanaṃ ca yathoktaṃ brūyāt prāṇābādhe 'pi dṛṣṭe ||
children.translated_text: And he should deliver the royal message exactly as instructed, even when danger to life is evident.

children.text: parasya vāci vaktre dṛṣṭyāṃ ca prasādaṃ vākyapūjanam iṣṭaparipraśnaṃ guṇakathāsaṅgam āsannam āsanaṃ satkāram iṣṭeṣu smaraṇaṃ viśvāsagamanaṃ ca lakṣayet tuṣṭasya viparītam atuṣṭasya ||
children.translated_text: In the other's speech, face, and gaze he should observe favor, honoring of his words, questions about what is dear, attachment to speaking of his virtues, a nearby seat, respectful treatment, remembrance among those who are favored, and the growth of trust as signs of satisfaction; the opposites are signs of dissatisfaction.

children.text: taṃ brūyāt dūtamukhā hi rājānaḥ tvaṃ cānye ca ||
children.translated_text: He should say to him, 'Kings have envoys as their mouths, you and others alike.'

children.text: tasmād udyateṣvapi śastreṣu yathoktaṃ vaktāro dūtāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, even when weapons are raised, envoys speak exactly as they have been instructed.

children.text: teṣām antāvasāyino 'pyavadhyāḥ kim aṅga punar brāhmaṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among them, even men of the lowest settlements are not to be killed, much less Brahmins.
This is the statement to the other ruler.
Such is the <s>dūta-dharma</s> (duty of an envoy).
If he has not been dismissed, he should remain, but should not become arrogant because of honors.
He should not think himself powerful among enemies.
He should endure unpleasant speech.
He should avoid women and drink.
He should sleep alone.
For knowledge of a person's disposition is seen in those who are asleep or intoxicated.

children.text: kṛtyapakṣopajāpam akṛtyapakṣe gūḍhapraṇidhānaṃ rāgāparāgau bhartari randhraṃ ca prakṛtīnāṃ tāpasavaidehakavyañjanābhyām upalabheta tayor antevāsibhiścikitsakapāṣaṇḍavyañjanobhayavetanair vā ||
children.translated_text: Through agents disguised as ascetics and merchants, or through their pupils, physicians, disguised heretics, or agents paid by both sides, he should ascertain the winning over of the faction fit to be won over, the secret placement of agents in the faction not fit to be won over, the affection and disaffection of the constituent elements toward their master, and their weak point.

children.text: teṣām asaṃbhāṣāyāṃ yācakamattonmattasuptapralāpaiḥ puṇyasthānadevagṛhacitralekhyasaṃjñābhir vā cāram upalabheta ||
children.translated_text: If he cannot converse with them, he should obtain intelligence through the utterances of beggars, drunkards, madmen, and sleepers, or through signs in holy places, temples, pictures, and writing.
When someone has been identified, he should proceed to win him over.

children.text: pareṇa coktaḥ svāsāṃ prakṛtīnāṃ pramāṇaṃ nācakṣīta ||
children.translated_text: And when questioned by the enemy, he should not disclose the measure of his own constituent elements.

children.text: sarvaṃ veda bhavān iti brūyāt kāryasiddhikaraṃ vā ||
children.translated_text: He should say, 'You know everything, sir,' or else say what brings about success in the matter.

children.text: kāryasyāsiddhāv uparudhyamānastarkayet kiṃ bhartur me vyasanam āsannaṃ paśyan svaṃ vā vyasanaṃ pratikartukāmaḥ pārṣṇigrāham āsāram antaḥkopam āṭavikaṃ vā samutthāpayitukāmaḥ mitram ākrandaṃ vā vyāghātayitukāmaḥ svaṃ vā parato vigraham antaḥkopam āṭavikaṃ vā pratikartukāmaḥ saṃsiddhaṃ vā me bhartur yātrākālam abhihantukāmaḥ sasyapaṇyakupyasaṃgrahaṃ durgakarma balasamuddhānaṃ vā kartukāmaḥ svasainyānāṃ vā vyāyāmasya deśakālāvākāṅkṣamāṇaḥ paribhavapramādābhyāṃ vā saṃsargānubandhārthī vā mām uparuṇaddhi iti ||
children.translated_text: If the mission has not succeeded and he is being detained, he should reason: 'Does he detain me because he sees some calamity close to my master; or because he wants to counteract his own calamity; or because he wants to stir up a rear-enemy, a rear-supporter, internal rebellion, or a forest chief; or because he wants to obstruct an ally or a rescuer; or because he wants to counteract a war against himself from another, an internal rebellion, or a forest trouble; or because he wants to strike at the prepared expedition time of my master; or because he wants to gather grain, merchandise, and raw materials, carry out fortress works, or raise forces; or because he is waiting for the proper place and time for exercising his own army; or because of contempt or carelessness, or because he seeks a continuing connection?'
Having understood this, he should remain or depart.
Or he should consider the desired purpose.

children.text: śāsanam aniṣṭam uktvā bandhavadhabhayād avisṛṣṭo 'pyapagacchet anyathā niyamyeta ||
children.translated_text: After delivering an unwelcome message, he should depart even if not dismissed, from fear of imprisonment or death; otherwise he may be restrained.
Sending messages, maintaining treaties, display of power, and gathering allies;
secret incitement, division among friends, and the transmission of hidden punishment;
carrying off relatives and precious things, knowledge through spies, and bold action;
settlement and release: these are the envoy's tasks and the basis of his operation.
He should have this done by his own envoys, and should keep watch over enemy envoys
by counter-envoys, secret agents, and visible and invisible guards.

children.text: rakṣito rājā rājyaṃ rakṣatyāsannebhyaḥ parebhyaśca pūrvaṃ dārebhyaḥ putrebhyaśca ||
children.translated_text: Protected, the king protects the kingdom from those nearby and from enemies, first from his wives and sons.
We shall explain the protection of wives in connection with the secret watch over the inner apartments.
But the protection of sons is as follows.
From birth onward he should guard royal sons.
For royal sons have the nature of crabs: they devour their begetter.

children.text: teṣām ajātasnehe pitaryupāṃśudaṇḍaḥ śreyān iti bhāradvājaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For those whose affection for their father has not yet arisen, <s>upāṃśudaṇḍa</s> (secret punishment) is better, says <s>Bhāradvāja</s>.
Killing one who has done no wrong is cruel, and it destroys the seed of the warrior line, says <s>Viśālākṣa</s>.
Therefore confinement in a single place is better.
This is the danger of a snake, say the <s>Pārāśaras</s>.

children.text: kumāro hi vikramabhayān māṃ pitāvaruṇaddhi iti jñātvā tam evāṅke kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: For the prince, knowing, "My father confines me because he fears my assault," would set his sights on that very father.
Therefore residence in the fortress of a frontier governor is better.
This is the danger of a ram, says <s>Piśuna</s>.

children.text: pratyāpatter hi tad eva kāraṇaṃ jñātvāntapālasakhaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: For, knowing that this very thing is the cause of his restoration, he would become a friend of the frontier governor.

children.text: tasmāt svaviṣayād apakṛṣṭe sāmantadurge vāsaḥ śreyān iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore residence in the fortress of a neighboring ruler, away from his own territory, is better.
This is the position of a calf, says <s>Kauṇapadanta</s>.

children.text: vatseneva hi dhenuṃ pitaram asya sāmanto duhyāt ||
children.translated_text: For the neighboring ruler would milk his father by means of him, just as one milks a cow by means of a calf.
Therefore residence among his maternal kinsmen is better.
This is the position of a banner, says <s>Vātavyādhi</s>.

children.text: tena hi dhvajenāditikauśikavad asya mātṛbāndhavā bhikṣeran ||
children.translated_text: For, with him as that banner, his maternal relatives would beg, like <s>Aditi-Kauśika</s>.
Therefore he should release him into village pleasures.

children.text: sukhoparuddhā hi putrāḥ pitaraṃ nābhidruhyanti iti ||
children.translated_text: For sons restrained by pleasure do not rebel against their father.
This is death while living, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.

children.text: kāṣṭham iva ghuṇajagdhaṃ rājakulam avinītaputram abhiyuktamātraṃ bhajyeta ||
children.translated_text: A royal family with an undisciplined son breaks as soon as it is attacked, like wood eaten by worms.

children.text: tasmād ṛtumatyāṃ mahiṣyām ṛtvijaścarum aindrābārhaspatyaṃ nirvapeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the chief queen is in her fertile season, the priests should offer a porridge oblation belonging to <s>Indra</s> and <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.

children.text: āpannasattvāyāḥ kaumārabhṛtyo garbhabharmaṇi prasave ca viyateta ||
children.translated_text: When she is pregnant, the keeper of princes should attend to the protection of the fetus and to the birth.
After she has given birth, the priest should perform the rites for a son.
When he is capable, those who know the matter should train him.

children.text: sattriṇām ekaścainaṃ mṛgayādyūtamadyastrībhiḥ pralobhayet pitari vikramya rājyaṃ gṛhāṇa iti ||
children.translated_text: One of the secret agents should entice him with hunting, gambling, liquor, and women, saying, "Attack your father and seize the kingdom."
Another secret agent should restrain him; so say the <s>Āmbhīyas</s>.
Awakening one who has not understood is a great fault, says <s>Kauṭilya</s>.

children.text: navaṃ hi dravyaṃ yena yenārthajātenopadihyate tat tad ācūṣati ||
children.translated_text: For new material absorbs whatever kind of substance it is smeared with.

children.text: evam ayaṃ navabuddhir yad yad ucyate tat tatśāstropadeśam ivābhijānāti ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, this person of fresh understanding regards whatever is said to him as instruction from the science.

children.text: tasmād dharmyam arthyaṃ cāsyopadiśen nādharmyam anarthyaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Therefore one should teach him what accords with <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>, not what is contrary to <s>dharma</s> and harmful.

children.text: sattriṇastvenaṃ tava smaḥ iti vadantaḥ pālayeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: But secret agents, saying, "We are yours," should guard him.

children.text: yauvanotsekāt parastrīṣu manaḥ kurvāṇam āryāvyañjanābhiḥ strībhir amedhyābhiḥ śūnyāgāreṣu rātrāv udvejayeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: When, through the excitement of youth, he turns his mind to other men's wives, they should terrify him at night in empty houses with impure women disguised as respectable women.
When he desires liquor, they should terrify him by means of a drugged drink.
When he desires gambling, they should terrify him through tricksters.
When he desires hunting, they should frighten him with men disguised as obstructors.

children.text: pitari vikramabuddhiṃ tathā ityanupraviśya bhedayeyuḥ aprārthanīyo rājā vipanne ghātaḥ sampanne narakapātaḥ saṃkrośaḥ prajābhir ekaloṣṭavadhaśca iti ||
children.translated_text: If he has the idea of attacking his father, they should enter into it by saying, "So be it," and then split him away from it: "Kingship is not to be desired; if it fails there is death, if it succeeds there is a fall into hell, denunciation by the subjects, and death by a single clod."
They should make him feel aversion.
A beloved only son he should confine.

children.text: bahuputraḥ pratyantam anyaviṣayaṃ vā preṣayed yatra garbhaḥ paṇyaṃ ḍimbo vā na bhavet ||
children.translated_text: If he has many sons, he should send one to a frontier or to another territory, where there would be no source of offspring, wealth, or revolt.
One endowed with personal qualities he should appoint to the command of the army or to the position of heir apparent.
The distinctions among sons are: intelligent, of teachable understanding, and evil-minded.

children.text: śiṣyamāṇo dharmārthāv upalabhate cānutiṣṭhati ca buddhimān ||
children.translated_text: The intelligent one, when instructed, understands <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s> and also practices them.
The one of teachable understanding understands them, but does not practice them.
The evil-minded one is constantly given to harmful courses and hates <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>.
If that one is an only son, he should make an effort for the birth of another son.
Or he should produce sons through an appointed daughter.

children.text: vṛddhastu vyādhito vā rājā mātṛbandhukulyaguṇavatsāmantānām anyatamena kṣetre bījam utpādayet ||
children.translated_text: But an aged or diseased king should have seed produced in the field by one among maternal relatives, clansmen, virtuous men, or neighboring rulers.
And he should not establish an undisciplined only son in the kingdom.
When there are many sons, the confinement of one is possible; the father should act for the good of his sons.
Except in an emergency, sovereignty is honored as the share of the eldest.

children.text: kulasya vā bhaved rājyaṃ kulasaṃgho hi durjayaḥ
children.translated_text: Or the kingdom may belong to the family, for a confederation of the family is hard to conquer.
Unafflicted by the calamity of having no king, it dwells upon the earth forever.

children.text: vinīto rājaputraḥ kṛcchravṛttir asadṛśe karmaṇi niyuktaḥ pitaram anuvarteta anyatra prāṇabādhakaprakṛtikopakapātakebhyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A disciplined prince, living in hardship and assigned to work unsuited to him, should obey his father, except in matters involving danger to life, anger of the constituents, or sin.

children.text: puṇye karmaṇi niyuktaḥ puruṣam adhiṣṭhātāraṃ yācet ||
children.translated_text: When assigned to meritorious work, he should request a man as supervisor.
And, supervised by that man, he should carry out the command with special excellence.

children.text: abhirūpaṃ ca karmaphalam aupāyanikaṃ ca lābhaṃ pitur upanāyayet ||
children.translated_text: He should bring to his father a fitting result of the work and a gain suitable as a present.

children.text: tathāpyatuṣyantam anyasmin putre dāreṣu vā snihyantam araṇyāyāpṛccheta ||
children.translated_text: If even then his father is not pleased, and is attached to another son or to his wives, he should ask permission to go to the forest.

children.text: bandhavadhabhayād vā yaḥ sāmanto nyāyavṛttir dhārmikaḥ satyavāgavisaṃvādakaḥ pratigrahītā mānayitā cābhipannānāṃ tam āśrayeta ||
children.translated_text: Or, from fear of bondage or death, he should seek refuge with a neighboring ruler who is just in conduct, righteous, truthful, not deceitful, and one who receives and honors those who come to him.

children.text: tatrasthaḥ kośadaṇḍasampannaḥ pravīrapuruṣakanyāsambandham aṭavīsambandhaṃ kṛtyapakṣopagrahaṃ ca kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: Established there, and provided with treasury and army, he should form alliances with brave men and maidens, connections with forest people, and support among persons fit for action and their factions.
If he goes about alone, he should live by the occupations of refining gold, coloring gems, and dealing in gold, silver, merchandise, mines, and workshops.

children.text: pāṣaṇḍasaṃghadravyam aśrotriyopabhogyaṃ vā devadravyam āḍhyavidhavādravyaṃ vā gūḍham anupraviśya sārthayānapātrāṇi ca madanarasayogenātisaṃdhāyāpaharet ||
children.translated_text: Having secretly entered, he should carry off the property of associations of sectarians, or temple property used by those who are not <s>śrotriyas</s>, or the property of a wealthy widow, and also caravan conveyances and vessels, deceiving them by the use of an intoxicating preparation.
Or he should undertake a stratagem connected with a village beyond the frontier.
Or he should act with the support of his mother's attendants.

children.text: kāruśilpikuśīlavacikitsakavāgjīvanapāṣaṇḍacchadmabhir vā naṣṭarūpastadvyañjanasakhaśchidreṣu praviśya rājñaḥ śastrarasābhyāṃ prahṛtya brūyāt aham asau kumāraḥ sahabhogyam idaṃ rājyam eko nārhati bhoktum ye kāmayante māṃ bhartuṃ tān ahaṃ dviguṇena bhaktavetanenopasthāsyāmi iti
children.translated_text: Or, with his appearance changed, under the disguises of artisans, craftsmen, actors, physicians, professional speakers, and sectarians, and with friends bearing the same marks, he should enter through vulnerable points, strike the king with weapon or poison, and say: "I am that prince. This kingdom is to be enjoyed in common; one man does not deserve to enjoy it alone. Those who wish to support me, I shall maintain with double rations and wages."
Thus the conduct of a confined prince.

children.text: aparuddhaṃ tu mukhyaputrāpasarpāḥ pratipādyānayeyuḥ mātā vā pratigṛhītā ||
children.translated_text: But agents who are sons of chief men should win over a confined prince and bring him back; or his mother, once won over, should do so.
If he has been abandoned, secret agents should kill him by weapon or poison.
